analysis.one_liner: Raises prison time and fines for employers who willfully violate workplace safety laws.
analysis.headline: The bill would have raised the top prison sentence for a willful workplace safety violation causing a worker's death from one year to 20 years, but it died on the Senate calendar without ever getting a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have sharply increased criminal penalties under the Occupational Safety and Health Act: prison terms for willful violations that kill or seriously injure workers would rise from months to as much as 20 years, and fixed fines of $10,000–$20,000 would be replaced with much larger fines set under federal sentencing law. It would also have made company directors and officers personally liable for willfully authorizing safety violations and barred companies from paying their fines for them. The Senate Labor Committee approved it in August 1990, but it never came to a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in dangerous jobs and their families, who would gain a real deterrent: an employer that willfully ignores safety rules and kills or seriously injures a worker would face prison time measured in years rather than months, executives could be held personally liable, and companies could no longer pick up the tab for a convicted executive's fine.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum prison term for a willful OSHA violation causing an employee's death from six months for a first offense (one year for a repeat offense) to 10 years and 20 years respectively.
Creates a new crime for willful safety violations that cause serious bodily injury short of death, punishable by up to 7 years in prison, or up to 14 years for repeat offenders.
Creates a new crime for willful violations that recklessly endanger workers' lives, punishable by up to 5 years in prison (10 for repeat offenders) in the version introduced.
Replaces the old fixed maximum fines of $10,000 and $20,000 with fines set under 18 U.S.C. 3571, the federal sentencing provision that allows far larger criminal fines.

Makes directors, officers, and agents who willfully authorize, order, or carry out a safety violation subject to the same fines and prison terms, and prohibits companies from paying those fines out of corporate assets on their behalf.
Confirms that state and local prosecutors remain free to bring their own criminal cases over workplace deaths and injuries, so federal law would not crowd out tougher state prosecution.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that willfully violate OSHA safety standards and the executives who authorize those violations: they would face multi-year prison terms, potentially much larger fines, and personal liability that can no longer be reimbursed by the company. Employers that comply with safety rules would bear essentially no new cost, since every new penalty requires a willful violation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers who willfully break safety laws

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'serious bodily injury' broadly, including unconsciousness, extreme physical pain, and protracted disfigurement, which could expose employers to felony charges for serious accidents that fall short of the most egregious conduct.
The personal liability provision reaches executives found to have merely 'acquiesced' in a violation, extending individual criminal liability to people who did not personally commit the unsafe act.

The version the committee approved was narrower than the bill as introduced: it dropped the new offense for willful violations that recklessly endanger workers, leaving only violations causing serious bodily injury.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For working people the upside is large: under the 1970 law, an employer who willfully violated a safety rule and killed a worker faced at most six months to a year in prison, a penalty widely seen as no deterrent at all; this bill would have made that a felony carrying up to 20 years. The costs fall almost entirely on violators and their executives, which is the point. The honest concerns are about breadth: a very broad definition of serious bodily injury and liability for executives who merely acquiesce could pull ordinary serious accidents into criminal court, and the committee had already begun trimming the bill for that reason.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Labor Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar in August 1990, but no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the bill on February 21, 1990, with Senators Mikulski, Simon, Adams, and Kennedy, and it was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The Labor Subcommittee held hearings on May 1, 1990.
On June 27, 1990 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment, and on August 1, 1990 Senator Kennedy reported it to the Senate with a written report.

The committee substitute dropped the new offense for willful violations that recklessly endanger workers, keeping the new serious-bodily-injury offense, the higher penalties, and the ban on corporate payment of executives' fines.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 755) on August 1, 1990, and received no further action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and executives who willfully violate workplace safety laws are better off, because they continue to face only the 1970 law's maximum penalties of six months to one year in prison and small fixed fines instead of multi-year prison terms and personal liability. Workers injured or killed by willful violations gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and executives facing safety-law liability

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the Senate Labor Committee.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate with a substitute amendment on August 1, 1990.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it sat on the legislative calendar from August 1990 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Employer and business associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanding criminal penalties for OSHA violations and personal liability for executives.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so positions on the floor are unknown; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats and the Democratic-led committee reported the bill, while the Democratic Senate leadership never scheduled it.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (manufacturing, construction, mining)
industries.note: The bill would expose them to prison-scale penalties, with maximum terms rising from months to as much as 20 years, for willful safety violations that kill or seriously injure workers. Because the bill died, they remain subject to the 1970 law's maximum of six months to one year.

Executives who willfully authorize or acquiesce in safety violations would face the same fines and prison terms as the company, and the company would be barred from paying their fines for them. The bill's defeat preserves their insulation from personal criminal exposure under OSHA.
